neutral_facts.value: The accused were involved in an incident where the victim, a social worker, was sitting in a Ganesh festival pandal and was talking with another individual. Two unknown persons entered the pandal, opened fire on the victim, and shot him multiple times at point blank range. The victim was taken to a hospital and declared dead upon arrival. The injured eyewitness, who was also present, was shot and fell unconscious. The prosecution relied on eyewitness testimonies and a test identification parade (TIP) to identify the accused. However, the TIP was conducted with significant delays and inconsistencies, leading to doubts about the reliability of the identification. The trial court convicted the accused based on the testimonies of five eyewitnesses and the TIP, but the High Court overturned the conviction, citing flaws in the evidence and the TIP process.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the trial court's conviction was well reasoned and well considered, and that the evidence of eye-witnesses and the Test Identification Parade (TIP) conclusively established that Al and Al 2 had fired on the deceased, with the recovery of the weapon and ballistic report further strengthening the case.

quotes.text: The Trial Court found that the prosecution has proved its case beyond reasonable doubt and hence the accused were convicted of the offences charged after being found guilty.
The recovery of the weapon along with the ballistic report further strengthens the conclusion.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the eye-witness testimonies suffered various infirmities, contradictions, and the TIP was not conducted properly and was delayed, thus the High Court rightly granted the benefit of doubt to the accused as their identity was not clearly established by the prosecution.

quotes.text: The High Court is of the view that the Trial Court had placed unwarranted reliance on the Test Identification Parades in arriving at the guilt of the accused when the same suffered major discrepancies along with the inconsistencies of the depositions of the eyewitnesses to that of the injured eyewitness' testimony.
The High Court rightly granted benefit of doubt to the accused as their identity was not clearly established by prosecution.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that when an attack is made on the injured/deceased by a mob in a crowded place and the eyewitnesses had little time to see the accused, the substantive evidence should be sufficiently corroborated by a test identification parade held soon after the occurrence, and any delay in holding the test identification parade may be fatal to the prosecution case.
